summary:
Mars Explorer is a research-oriented planetary exploration and mission operations platform designed to evaluate candidate surface traverses on Mars. The application unifies multi-mission NASA orbital and surface archives—including HiRISE elevation models, USGS Jezero chronostratigraphy, and atmospheric measurements from Curiosity and Perseverance—into an interactive planning environment.

Following a four-stage workflow (Investigate → Plan → Explore → Report), users evaluate scientific questions with orbital evidence, plot traverse routes with dynamic slope-hazard and stratigraphic contact analysis, and explore regional terrains (Jezero, Gale, Valles Marineris, and Olympus Mons) in a first-person 3D WebGL EVA simulator driven by 0.38g suit bioenergetics. Completed traverses and sample logs compile into an Expedition Dossier with a strict 4-tier provenance audit, providing an extensible research and simulation foundation for future crewed planetary exploration studies.
details:
1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

Mars Explorer guides users through an authentic four-stage planetary flight-readiness workflow:

Stage 01: Investigate (Scientific Evidence Inspector)

  • Hypothesis & Gap Identification: Researchers formulate mission objectives and inspect targeted Martian environments (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris).
  • Multispectral & In-Situ Analysis: Users analyze NASA MRO CRISM hyperspectral mineral signatures (identifying clays, carbonates, and olivine), inspect MGS TES thermal inertia/albedo, and query Mars 2020 Perseverance MEDA and MSL Curiosity REMS diurnal atmospheric logs (surface pressure, temperature fluctuations, UV radiation).

Stage 02: Plan (EVA Traverse & Stratigraphy Planner)

  • Precision Topographic Plotting: Mission planners drop EVA waypoints directly onto high-resolution USGS/NASA CTX 20m Digital Elevation Models (DEMs).
  • Automated Geologic Contact Detection: As waypoints are connected, the system cross-references vector coordinates against the peer-reviewed USGS SIM 3464 chronostratigraphic map, automatically alerting astronauts when their traverse crosses geological boundaries (e.g., transitioning from the olivine-rich Māaz Formation onto the Western Delta scarp).
  • Slope & Hazard Profiling: The elevation engine computes real-time terrain gradients, issuing automated warnings for steep inclines (>15∘>15^\circ>15∘) and non-navigable hazards (>25∘>25^\circ>25∘).

Stage 03: Explore (Interactive 3D EVA Surface Simulator)

  • First-Person Surface Walk: Users step onto the Martian surface in an interactive, hardware-accelerated 3D WebGL simulator powered by Three.js.
  • Astronaut Helmet HUD: Displays real-time heading, pitch, elevation relative to the MOLA areoid datum, and active geological unit identification.
  • Bioenergetics Life Support Engine: Life support drawdowns (O2O_2O2​ consumption, battery power, suit thermal pressure) are dynamically modeled using NASA SP-2008-548 (Apollo Lunar Surface EVA standards) scaled to Martian gravity (0.38g0.38g0.38g), incorporating metabolic expenditure penalties for astronaut speed, suit mass, and terrain grade.
  • In-Situ Geological Sampling: Astronauts collect rock and soil samples, log field observations, and place surface waypoints.

Stage 04: Review & Report (Expedition Dossier)

  • Automated Archiving: All traverse metrics, spectral findings, hazard warnings, environmental logs, and field samples are synthesized into a formal, peer-reviewable Scientific Expedition Dossier.
  • Open Formats: Dossiers can be reviewed interactively or exported directly to Markdown, JSON, and print-ready PDF.

🚀 Quick Start Guide (How to Test & Experience)

  1. Launch the Explorer: From the landing page, click "Start Exploration" to enter the mission dashboard.
  2. Select an Exploration Site: Choose Jezero Crater (or Gale Crater / Olympus Mons).
  3. Inspect the Data (Stage 1): Open the Evidence Inspector to examine real CRISM spectral mineral absorption bands and Perseverance MEDA temperature/pressure logs.
  4. Plan an EVA Traverse (Stage 2): In the Route Planner, click on the map to place 3–4 waypoints from the crater floor toward the western delta. Observe the elevation profile update in real time and watch the Geologic Unit Crossing indicator detect unit transitions.
  5. Simulate the EVA (Stage 3): Click "Launch EVA Simulation". Use W/A/S/D to navigate and your mouse to look around. Walk uphill and observe how your O2O_2O2​ and metabolic burn rate increase on the Helmet HUD. Press the sample key to collect geological specimens.
  6. Compile Dossier (Stage 4): Head to the Expedition Report tab to view your complete mission summary, telemetry logs, and export your flight-readiness dossier.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Bridges the Data-to-Operations Divide: Most planetary science tools are either raw, complex GIS desktop suites (requiring gigabyte downloads and specialized training) or simplified video games lacking scientific fidelity. Mars Explorer bridges this gap by making calibrated NASA science operational in a browser.
  • Zero-Install Web Accessibility: Runs smoothly on standard consumer hardware and mobile browsers without plugins, external software installations, or license fees.
  • Operational Training for Analog Missions: Provides analog habitats (e.g., Mars Desert Research Station, AMADEE) with a turnkey, standardized digital flight planning workspace that simulates real bioenergetics and terrain safety constraints.
  • Interdisciplinary Educational Power: Enables university classrooms to teach Martian deltaic sedimentology, landing site selection, and orbital spectrometry simultaneously.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  • Advancing NASA’s TOPS (Transform to Open Science) Initiative: Fulfills NASA’s commitment to open science by transforming multi-mission archives (PDS Geosciences Node, Mars Trek) into intuitive, interactive public research tools.
  • Empowering Analog Astronaut Crews: Serves as a free, open-source EVA traverse planner for analog astronaut field stations to pre-plan fieldwork paths and test consumables safety margins before stepping out of the airlock.
  • STEM & Citizen Science Democratization: Lowers the barrier of entry for students, amateur astronomers, and independent researchers to interact with authentic Mars exploration datasets without requiring institutional GIS licenses.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Frontend Architecture & UI:
    • Core Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Router v7.
    • Styling & Assets: Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide React icons.
    • 2D Mapping & GIS: Leaflet & React-Leaflet (NASA Mars Trek WMTS tile layer management, coordinate projections, and bounding-box queries).
    • 3D Surface & Planetary Rendering: Three.js, React Three Fiber (R3F), Drei, and Cesium (interactive 3D globe transitions, WebGL terrain chunk streaming, and first-person astronaut EVA controls).
    • API & Runtime: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX (async services for DEM chunk retrieval, tile indexing, and scientific layer metadata).
    • Data Processing: GeoTIFF, NumPy, and Rasterio (geospatial coordinate transforms, elevation profile extraction, and downsampling of USGS/MRO digital elevation models).
    • Google Gemini & OpenAI Codex: Utilized during the development lifecycle for planetary science literature research (PDS standards, Apollo bioenergetics models), automated test suite generation, cross-module type verification, and debugging complex geospatial coordinate transforms and 3D elevation interpolation math.
    • Data & Auth: Supabase (mission state persistence, session caching, and authentication).
    • Deployment: Cloudflare Pages (via Wrangler edge deployment) and Vercel-ready static builds.
    • Standard modern web browsers with hardware-accelerated WebGL 2.0 support (fully compatible across standard laptops, desktops, and mobile/tablet hardware without custom plugins).

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

  • Gamified Scientific Rigor: Instead of fictitious health meters, astronaut survival is tied directly to real-world bioenergetic physics (NASA SP-2008-548 Apollo metabolic rate formulas adjusted for Martian 0.38g0.38g0.38g and slope friction).
  • Multi-Scale Continuity (Orbit to Bootprints): Connects macro-scale global orbital imagery (232 m/pixel232\text{ m/pixel}232 m/pixel Viking mosaics) down to micro-scale surface photography (centimeter-level Perseverance Mastcam-Z images) and first-person 3D EVA traverses within a single coherent workflow.
  • Dynamic Stratigraphic Intelligence: The route planner doesn't just measure distance—it acts as an automated field geologist, detecting boundaries from the peer-reviewed USGS SIM 3464 map and alerting astronauts when they cross from igneous crater floors to lacustrine delta deposits.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Planetary Geodesy & Areocentric Coordinates: Mars is an oblate spheroid, not Earth. We discarded naive planar Euclidean approximations and anchored all planetary coordinates to the IAU areocentric Mars 2000 coordinate system, referencing elevations directly to the MOLA areoid datum (R=3,396.0 kmR = 3,396.0\text{ km}R=3,396.0 km), rigorously validated against ground-truth benchmarks (Jezero crater floor at −2,540 m-2,540\text{ m}−2,540 m; Olympus Mons caldera at +21,229 m+21,229\text{ m}+21,229 m).
  • Fidelity vs. WebGL Performance: Streaming multi-gigabyte CTX/HiRISE DEMs into a browser crashes client memory. We engineered a Level-of-Detail (LOD) heightmap chunking pipeline that delivers sub-meter visual fidelity in the immediate EVA radius while sustaining steady 60 FPS60\text{ FPS}60 FPS frame rates.
  • Network Fault Tolerance: Public planetary endpoints can experience rate-limiting or latency spikes. We implemented resilient offline fallbacks, local vector caching, and fallback boundaries to ensure the application never crashes with 404 or 502 errors during live demos or offline fieldwork.
  • Human Factors & Mission Survivability: Astronaut safety guidelines dictated our metabolic expenditure model—accounting for thermal dissipation in a low-pressure CO2\text{CO}_2CO2​ atmosphere (∼600 Pa\sim 600\text{ Pa}∼600 Pa), bulky pressurized suit encumbrance (45 kg45\text{ kg}45 kg terrestrial equivalent), and slope-induced cardiorespiratory strain.

7. NASA & Open Data Integration

  • NASA Mars Trek WMTS: Dynamic global tile streaming of Viking Color Mosaic (Mars_Viking_MDIM21_ClrMosaic_global_232m), MGS MOLA Global Hillshade, and THEMIS Daytime Infrared mosaics.
  • USGS Astrogeology Science Center: Scientific Investigations Map 3464 (Sun & Stack, 2020) chronostratigraphic vector geology and 20m CTX Digital Elevation Models.
  • NASA PDS Geosciences Node: MRO CRISM MTRDR targeted hyperspectral cubes and MGS TES albedo and thermal inertia indices.
  • In-Situ Rover Telemetry & Imagery: Mars 2020 Perseverance MEDA and MSL Curiosity REMS environmental data bundles, integrated with Perseverance Mastcam-Z raw/EDR surface imagery referenced by Sol and drive location.

Disclaimer

Mars Explorer is an independent open-science research tool created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Planetary imagery, elevation data, and remote sensing datasets are courtesy of NASA, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL-Caltech), the United States Geological Survey (USGS Astrogeology), and the European Space Agency (ESA). This project is an independent educational submission and is not officially affiliated with or endorsed by NASA or the United States Government.
